title: Do Insects Matter More than People?
gist: A Hedgehog Review piece rebuts influencer-philosopher Matthew Adelstein's viral Substack claim that large aggregates of insects matter more than humans, arguing via modus tollens and the Moorean Shift that dissenters need no counter-argument when a conclusion is obviously false. It defends the nonfungible value of human life as more fundamental than any premises that could overturn it.

insights.claim: A small group of young public philosophers, including Princeton philosophy doctoral students, now operate as social-media influencers, blending academic roles with online performance.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Signals academia-to-Substack migration of intellectual influence; viral provocation is becoming a career channel for academics.

insights.claim: Matthew Adelstein, writing as 'Bentham's Bulldog', drew wide attention with a viral Substack post arguing that in sufficiently large aggregates insects matter more than people; the author attributes much of its appeal to its obvious perversity.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Illustrates how contrarian, bizarre claims drive engagement in the attention economy ('alvinizing').

themes.theme: Modus tollens and the Moorean Shift

insights.claim: A valid argument can be run backwards: if the conclusion is less plausible than the denial of the premises, modus tollens rationally rejects a premise, so dissenters need not produce a counter-argument.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: A general tool for resisting clever-but-wrong models: when outputs are absurd, reject inputs rather than accept the conclusion.

insights.claim: The Moorean Shift, after G.E. Moore, holds that arguments for radical claims fail when their premises are less plausible than the denial of their conclusion, acting as a 'Sword of Damocles' over arguments that unsettle plausible claims.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Useful heuristic for evaluating counterintuitive theses: weigh premise plausibility against conclusion plausibility.
insights.quote: chastening all arguments that would pretend to unsettle plausible claims on the basis of less plausible premises
insights.locator: None of this is controversial or novel.

insights.claim: Insisting that dissenters are rationally outmatched unless they present an explicit argument is a dialectical trick that may put opponents on the back foot but has no rational force.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Warns against conceding to whoever has the more elaborate argument; rhetorical structure is not evidence.
insights.quote: nothing more than a dialectical trick

insights.claim: No one can argue for all premises without infinite regress, so basic ethical arguments ultimately rest on intuitions; Adelstein's own unargued premises include that sentient experience grounds worth and a 'veil of ignorance' assumption that we might have been insects.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Every model bottoms out in assumptions; scrutinize the unstated ones in effective-altruism-style aggregation arguments.

insights.claim: The author contends Adelstein's conclusion is not merely weird but obviously false: human life has special, nonfungible value reflected on at length by civilization and embedded implicitly in legal codes and humanistic traditions.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Pushback against utilitarian aggregation (e.g., insect-welfare prioritization) that could otherwise steer philanthropic or policy resources.

insights.claim: Rationally unsettling the irreplaceability of human life would require premises at least as fundamental as that claim itself, which the author doubts can be done and says Adelstein has not done.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Implies insect-over-human arguments will remain fringe rather than reshape mainstream ethics.

insights.claim: Resistance to the insect thesis does not stem from a low view of insects — the author, a childhood would-be entomologist, prizes them — but from appreciating the overriding superiority of the human being.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Separates animal-welfare sympathy from acceptance of aggregative utilitarian conclusions.
